project.name: Health Supply Chain Network Design
project.summary: A living map of a country's health supply chain that shows what it costs to reach every clinic — by road, boat and plane, month by month — and who gets left out when money is saved.

features.name: Usable by everyone
features.oneLiner: The whole screen works with a keyboard, reads correctly aloud, and holds up on a small display.

needsYou.title: The design work is finished and waiting on you
needsYou.text: All 23 accessibility checks and 288 automatic tests pass. It is saved on its own copy and has not joined the main project. Nothing is deployed anywhere yet.

stories.title: Use the whole tool with only a keyboard
stories.note: Six controls used to be mouse-only and silent to a screen reader.

stories.title: Read every label and figure clearly
stories.note: The faint grey most explanations were written in was too pale to read.

stories.title: Use it on a touch screen
stories.note: Buttons stay small for a mouse and grow to finger size only on a touch screen.

stories.title: Have it checked automatically so it cannot quietly break
stories.note: 23 checks, run with one command, and they fail loudly.

stories.title: Use it comfortably on a phone
stories.unsure: It stacks and stays usable below 768 pixels, but has had no phone-first design pass.

decisions.what: Buttons stay small for a mouse and grow to finger size only on a touch screen, so neither gets a compromise.
The accessibility check runs itself and fails loudly, so this cannot quietly rot later.

unsure: There is no light-colour version of the screen — it is dark only.

activity.what: All 23 checks passed, on all nine panels, at six screen widths
Six controls that only worked with a mouse now work with a keyboard too

features.name: The map
features.oneLiner: Every clinic, store and delivery route in the country on one screen you can read at a glance.

stories.title: See every clinic, store and delivery route on one map
Read the map with no internet connection at all
stories.unsure: The coastline we draw is rough — good to about 4km. Fine for showing where things are, not for measuring.

stories.title: Colour the map by how well each clinic is supplied
Switch on a detailed online map when there is a connection

decisions.what: The map must work with no internet at all. A provincial office often has none, so the coastline ships with the tool and online maps are an optional extra on top.
Decided against switching to Mapbox. It needs internet and a paid key, and would not change any answer the tool gives.

activity.what: Looked at using Mapbox instead and decided the current approach is better here
Ten real towns were being marked as out at sea — the coastline was wrong and is now fixed

features.name: Comparing plans side by side
features.oneLiner: Run several 'what if' plans at once and see cost, coverage and risk in one table.

stories.title: Compare several 'what if' plans side by side
stories.note: Today's network costs 11.24M kina a year and reaches everyone.

stories.title: Run every plan at once instead of waiting for each
See how each plan differs from how things work today
Download the comparison as a spreadsheet

decisions.what: Instead of forcing every plan to reach everyone, we put a price on not reaching someone. Every plan now gives an answer you can read, rather than some simply failing.

unsure: The costs, demand and boat timetables in the demo are illustrative, not the ministry's real figures. The clinic locations and the shape of the network are real.

activity.what: Running seven plans at once was occasionally failing — found the cause and fixed it
Opening three new stores looked like it cost 4.5M a year more than it does — a one-off building cost was being counted as a yearly bill

features.name: Who pays for a saving
features.oneLiner: Shows which communities lose their supply when a plan saves money — before anyone decides.

stories.title: See which communities lose supply when a plan saves money
stories.note: Cutting cost by 19.5% moves 217,480 people from supplied to not supplied.

stories.title: See the number of people affected, not just a percentage
Set a floor that no community can fall below
stories.note: Holding the hardest-to-reach fifth at 90% still saves 9.3%.

decisions.what: Fairness is part of the sum, not a report at the end. A plan that saves money by giving up on the hardest-to-reach fifth has to say so in the same breath.

unsure: How we decide which communities are hardest to reach is our own definition. A ministry may well use a different one, and can change it.

activity.what: Checked the numbers hold up both ways round — the saving and the abandonment are the same figure seen from two sides

features.name: Month by month conditions
features.oneLiner: See what the wet season does — which roads close, and who can only be reached by plane.

stories.title: See which routes close in each month of the year
Re-price a whole plan for a single month
stories.note: In February 19 clinics cannot be reached at all and the plan costs 35.8% more.

stories.title: See who can only be reached by plane in the wet season

decisions.what: Every route carries twelve monthly access figures from the start, so the seasons are built in rather than bolted on later.

unsure: The seasonal patterns come from typical weather, not from records of roads actually closing. Worth checking with provincial staff before publishing anything.

activity.what: February and July had no workable answer at all — changed the approach so every month gives a readable result naming who is affected

features.name: Getting your own data in
features.oneLiner: Download a spreadsheet, fill it in, upload it back. It is checked before anything is saved.

stories.title: Download a blank template to fill in
See everything wrong with a file before any of it is saved
stories.note: 37 checks. Only six things are serious enough to stop an upload.

stories.title: Export everything back out again
stories.note: What you download and what you upload have identical columns.

stories.title: Start a new country without filling in 70 columns by hand
stories.unsure: Still nothing pre-fills a new country from open data. Only six fields are strictly required, but the workbook does not yet say which.

stories.title: Fix a flagged row without going back to the spreadsheet
stories.note: Correct it in the upload, it is re-checked immediately, and nothing is written until you apply.

decisions.what: Nothing is saved until you have seen the check results and said go ahead. A half-finished import is worse than one that stops, because nobody can tell which half is real.
What you download and what you upload have identical columns, so the work survives even if this tool does not.
Corrections happen inside the uncommitted upload, never against live data, so the two-step import stays the safety property it was.

unsure: Only Excel files are accepted. No CSV, and no older .xls.

activity.what: A clinic flagged 139 km out to sea can now be corrected in place and the block clears
Checked that exporting everything and importing it straight back changes nothing

features.name: Connecting to a country's own systems
features.oneLiner: Pull the clinic list and consumption straight out of the systems a ministry already runs.

stories.title: Pull the clinic list straight from DHIS2
stories.unsure: Only ever talked to a stand-in server we built, never a real ministry system.

stories.title: Pull from OpenLMIS
stories.unsure: Same — built and working, never tried against a real deployment.

stories.title: Pull from Open mSupply
stories.unsure: Papua New Guinea's own mSupply is an older version that does not offer this kind of connection.

stories.title: See every proposed change before anything is saved
stories.note: 6 clinics matched, 1 new, 1 moved, 1 renamed on the last run.

stories.title: Keep the delivery routes untouched when syncing
Keep passwords out of the tool entirely
stories.note: They can live outside it, so they never end up in a backup of it.

stories.title: Have a sync run on a schedule instead of by hand

decisions.what: A sync never touches the delivery routes. No stock system knows about boats, and losing the timetables would destroy the hardest part of the model to rebuild.

unsure: The whole feature needs one real ministry connection before anyone relies on it.

activity.what: A full pull, preview and save worked over a real network connection to a stand-in server
Two different clinics in the same town were being treated as one place because their names were trimmed too aggressively — fixed

features.name: The costed plan of action
features.oneLiner: Turns a chosen plan into a phased list of what to do, what it costs, and in what order.

stories.title: Turn a chosen plan into a phased list of what to do
See one-off costs separately from yearly running costs
Hand the plan to someone else as a document
stories.note: One self-contained HTML page that prints to PDF. Leads with the trade-off, names the people, states what it rests on.

decisions.what: One-off building costs are shown separately from yearly running costs, so a plan cannot look cheaper than it is.

unsure: How long each phase takes is an estimate, not drawn from how long this work actually takes in practice.

activity.what: A scenario can be handed over as a report rather than a spreadsheet
Checked the roadmap costs add up to the same total the plan reports

features.name: Selling this beyond one country
features.oneLiner: Turning a Papua New Guinea tool into something a consultant anywhere can pay to use.

stories.title: Set up a second country without a developer
stories.note: The coastline, terrain factors and seasonal profiles are country data now, not code.

stories.title: Sign in to your own account
stories.unsure: Nothing exists. Today anyone who reaches the tool can read and change everything in it.

stories.title: Pay for access
Hand a country over to a ministry when the work ends
stories.unsure: This is the promise the whole tool is sold on, and how the money would work is unresolved.

decisions.what: Wrote up what would have to be built and what the market looks like, including the parts that are uncomfortable.
A new country starts with a bounding box that rejects nothing. Inventing one would reject real facilities, which is worse than no check.

unsure: If the consultant is the one paying and the tool is meant to stay after they leave, who pays next year? Unresolved.
The consultants this would be sold to lost most of their funding in 2025. The need went up; the number of people with a budget went down.
The estimate of a few hundred people who would pay is our own guess, not a figure from anywhere.

activity.what: Opened a second country over the API with no code change, and its offshore check uses its own coastline
Wrote up what to build and what the market looks like, with the honest version of both

parkingLot.name: Mapbox as the map
parkingLot.note: Looked at properly and set aside. It needs an internet connection and a paid key, and roads carry only 11.5% of the cost in this model — so it would not change any answer. The reasoning is written down.

parkingLot.name: Better-looking offline map
parkingLot.note: A sharper map that still needs no internet. The genuinely useful version of the Mapbox idea we turned down. Nothing started.

parkingLot.name: Real road distances
parkingLot.note: The tool already has a place for this to plug into. Until it does, road distances are informed estimates and the tool says so on every one.

parkingLot.name: Collecting data on phones in the field
parkingLot.note: For countries where the information does not exist yet and has to be gathered. Would use the survey tools the sector already uses rather than a new app.

parkingLot.name: Accounts, logins and payment
parkingLot.note: Needed before anyone could pay for access. Planned out in detail, not begun — it is the first thing to build if the answer is yes.
